title: Recent Earthquakes Map: Latest Seismic Activity
description: See recent earthquakes on the map with the Recent Earthquakes Map — USGS-fed events with magnitude, depth and location for awareness and education. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, on a typical day the map carries dozens of fresh pins: the USGS locates roughly 500,000 earthquakes a year, though only about 100,000 are felt by anyone.
quick_answer: The Recent Earthquakes Map visualises the latest seismic events from open USGS earthquake feeds — magnitude, location, depth and time for quakes around the world. Open it for awareness and education: what shook, where, how deep and how strong, on the record of the world's most complete public seismic catalogue.
steps_intro: The planet's daily trembling, on one map:

body.t: The first question — was that an earthquake, and how big? — is answered here from the same feed officials use. Cross-check the epicentre against your location with the
's sibling distance tools if 'how far away?' follows.
Heading to Japan, Chile, Türkiye or Indonesia? A glance at recent activity frames the region's normal background — the Ring of Fire is a statistic before it is a headline.
A week of pins draws the plate boundaries more honestly than any textbook plate diagram — students watch subduction zones trace themselves.
Social feeds exaggerate magnitudes within minutes. The catalogue's reviewed values settle what actually happened and where the early numbers came from.

examples.label: Example · Magnitude is not a volume knob

body.t: Each whole magnitude step releases about 32 times more energy: a magnitude 6 releases roughly 1,000 times a magnitude 4's energy (32 × 32). The map's small pins and large pins live in different physical worlds that the shared scale politely flattens.

A magnitude 6 at 10 km depth under a city is a disaster; the same at 600 km under the ocean is a scientific notice. The feed's depth column is why the map shows more than dots — read it with the magnitude, always.

popular_table.intro: Published catalogue statistics — the background rate the map samples.
popular_table.note: Roughly 90% of the world's earthquakes occur around the Pacific 'Ring of Fire'. Depth classes: shallow under 70 km, intermediate 70–300 km, deep 300–700 km — the deepest quakes on record approach 700 km.

faq: USGS automatic solutions post within minutes for well-instrumented regions, then seismologists review and refine magnitude and location. Early pins can shift — the catalogue treats revision as honesty, not error.
Why do two sources report different magnitudes?
Magnitude has flavours (local ML, moment Mw, body-wave mb) computed from different signals; they agree roughly and differ in detail. Moment magnitude (Mw) is the reference for large events.
What is the largest ever recorded?
Magnitude 9.5, Chile, 1960 — the Valdivia earthquake, on the moment magnitude scale. The 2004 Sumatra (9.1) and 2011 Tōhoku (9.1) events follow it in the catalogue.

No — not the time-place-magnitude prediction the word implies. Science offers probabilities over decades ( hazard maps ) and seconds of early warning once one begins. Anyone selling prediction is selling fiction.
Does a swarm mean a big one is coming?

Statistically, most swarms end quietly; each magnitude-5 raises the short-term odds of a larger event modestly (aftershock sequences follow known laws, like Omori's and Båth's). Agencies communicate the numbers; the map shows the events.

Tsunami warnings come from dedicated centres (NOAA's PTWC and national agencies) within minutes for qualifying submarine quakes. This map is for awareness — warnings belong to the warning systems, loud and official.
The catalogue includes quarry blasts and induced events where networks classify them — depth near zero and odd hours are the usual tells, and the feed's event-type field says so where known.
This page's window is recent activity; the USGS catalogue search reaches back more than a century for the historical record — the 1906 San Francisco and 1811–12 New Madrid sequences included.
